Real-time well control during drilling (geosteering) depends on accurately interpreting subsurface position based on limited data from passing well logs. Because these logs are influenced by numerous uncertain drilling conditions, statistical machine learning is proposed here as a robust framework for analyzing them. This approach builds a model of the relationship between log readings and formation properties, facilitating well path visualization and deviation correction. The methodology employs a robust principal component analysis technique to separate principal components of the log data, distinguishing major patterns from outliers. Following this, a model is constructed using these components alongside multivariate uncertainty assessment. Ultimately, this study provides a working example using directional well data from a practical drilling operation.

Named entity recognition (NER) serves as a foundational task in natural language processing aimed at extracting named entities. Traditional NNER approaches treat extraction as a linear sequence labeling problem, employing algorithms like CRF to determine the most probable tag arrangement for a text. Although these methods have demonstrated efficacy, they generate a significant number of invalid outputs containing improper gaps within entities. To rectify this, this study proposes an innovative framework that interprets NNER as a holistic parsing job: instead of processing text word-by-word, it parses the sentence in syntactic order using a parse tree, with leaf nodes representing actual words. By adopting this strategy, the system can smoothly identify nested entity structures and enforce global consistency constraints to produce more structured, coherent results. Experimental data on two standard benchmarks confirms that this proposed approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methodologies.

Human teachers are instrumental in enabling rapid human learning for task execution involving robot agents, with acoustic delivery often proving more effective than written instructions for conveying actions to those robots. Although this finding supports accelerated learning, there remains a knowledge gap regarding how human facilitators acoustically guide robots on specific tasks. Our study compares and contrasts the acoustic characteristics of trained vs. untrained instructors guiding robots on manipulation challenges. We collected over three hours of audio from both untrained comparators and unbiassed facilitators performing the task themselves. Our analysis shows unbiassed facilitators spend more time providing positive acoustic feedback on task completion and utilize faster speech rates and higher pitch ranges when demonstrating tasks. These results offer a foundational understanding of how unbiassed facilitators behave acoustically in human teacher roles for task execution.

Automated form submission and extraction have long been effectively handled by web browsers, yet these capabilities have historically excluded artificial intelligence-driven conversational interfaces. Extending such automation machines to these platforms would substantially accelerate the processes for validating their correctness and maintaining performance. The primary obstacles to achieving this are the inherent unpredictability of user queries and the necessity for automation scripts to be automatically generated. To overcome these challenges, we present a behavioral abstraction model that accounts for the visual structure and dynamic functional elements of the target verification sites. This model enables the automatic creation of minimal execution scripts capable of rendering initial messages and processing automated answers based on user inputs, thereby enabling full automation. Additionally, we implemented a machine learning classifier to distinguish between six dominant types of user queries and the corresponding automation responses. Together, these methods form an automated testing framework that has been applied to various well-known chatbots to verify the system's effectiveness and feasibility for broader implementation.

Constrained within 200 AU by most models, the hypothetical mass of Planet X ($M_X$) is insufficient to generate detectable proper motion or position shifts. We postulate that $M_X$ could still be inferred from the orbital mechanics of known planets. Applying this framework, we demonstrate that a $M_X$ of 15 Earth masses is achievable by analyzing observable data. Specifically, such a body could account for the secular non-gravitational residuals observed in the tracking of Uranus and Neptune, and potentially explain acceleration trends currently noted for Venus and the Earth.

We further explore whether $M_X$ imprints on known trans-Neptunian anomalies, including the semi-major axis acceleration of Sedna, eccentricity fluctuations in Icaronid orbits, and historical inclination changes within Resonant Population bodies. We conclude by investigating whether the clustering of early Kuiper belt objects around 45,000 AU distance and 30-degree inclination can be attributed to this object.

Accurate assessment of neural machine translation (NMT) systems relies on interpreters who evaluate samples across various contexts, yet recruiting a large team is costly and inefficient, while doing so individually remains impractical. Furthermore, current commercial products fail to efficiently support translation evaluators with adequate tools and resources. To solve these problems, we propose an original approach to assist evaluation professionals by automating key archival processes such as collecting bilingual translation records and generating alignment diagrams, as well as creating search functionalities to help locate search results more easily. To do so, our approach depends upon an alignment diagram generation algorithm based upon a bipartite graph, which in effect offers a clever means to build up a bilingual alignment database solely from one-way (unilateral) machine translation records. Employing a diagram-based method for archive construction allows us to achieve superior results compared to competing strategies, especially in terms of precision when dealing with bilingual record searches that lack corresponding partners.

Furthermore, based on precise measurements of sigma-8 and H_0 within our current aeon, this work estimates the masses of remnant black holes from the predecessor universe, which are expected to have evaporated via Hawking mechanisms to achieve the massless condition. Deep learning frameworks have proven effective for computer vision in resource-abundant settings; however, their application in industry often transfers to scenarios where certain categories are well-documented and others are poorly documented. In these real-world contexts, it is practical and cost-efficient to collect multiple examples for each category by designating a "few-shot" or "prototype" category center, rather than expending effort on standard individual labeling. Consequently, this paper addresses few-shot learning, defining a few-shot category center as the representative center for that category. We note, however, that existing techniques stricken with the need to retrain or significant adjustments whenever a new center is desired. In contrast, this paper presents a method to learn type-based prompt centers so as not to require retiming whenever desired. Further, this paper establishes that class-type parts are desired to represent the desired corner while capturing the type's characteristic labeling. Finally, experiments prove that this proposed technique outperforms existing techniques by a large margin.

Recommendation systems for music albums frequently face challenges related to sparsity in multiple domains, stemming from users exhibiting limited sampling counts and inherent preferences difficult to capture. Consequently, existing approaches yield suboptimal performance. To mitigate these issues, this paper introduces a novel multi-sparse-domain collaborative filtering framework based on enhanced global attribute preference learning. The method leverages the homogeneity of musical tastes within the domain to aggregate sparse data points, while simultaneously establishing a feedback loop where inter-domain information supplements data integration. Specifically, we employ a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) model recommended for comprehensive learning of user and album features, utilizing both implicit interactions (recommendations) and explicit interactions (ratings) as input. An optimization strategy efficiently updates implicit preferences through explicit data, thereby refining recommendations. Additionally, to preserve privacy regarding user explicit feedback, we implement an encryption-decryption mechanism during feature extraction. Corresponding algorithms have been developed to execute this recommendation strategy, demonstrating its viability. Experimental outcomes confirm that this approach significantly surpasses the accuracy of state-of-the-art methods.

This project introduces the Python/JAX-based 'Hypatia.jl' library, designed to address convex optimization problems involving natural cones such as positive semidefiniteness, orthogonality, and conic positivity. The authors note that while the standard RCV toolkit offers broad support for optimization over the positive semidefinite cone, it lacks the ability to compose basic operations like the construction of orthogonal or cone-positive structures directly. This restriction hinders the modern development pattern of first declaratively defining a problem and only subsequently generating its system of equations. The Hypatia.jl package aims to fill this gap by enabling the direct formulation of problems within RCV, therewith enhancing the utility of the overall framework.

Brain MRI scanners deployed in clinical environments frequently suffer from performance degradation due to misaligned or partially clogged systems, which can compromise image clarity and diagnostic accuracy. While deep learning methods effectively automate infrared thermography monitoring, these models depend heavily on consistent MRI scanners performance, limiting their practical use. In this study, we address both unsupervised and semi-supervised approaches for sensor defects. Salamandre shows, for instance that end-to-end learning can identify MRI anomalies using only real-world data that does not require labeling; however, this method also requires labeling a relatively small subset of abnormal images. Conversely, the proposed Salamsan model, which uses a teacher-stitching configuration to train parallel supra-learned networks with additional annotations, achieves superior results compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques. These advancements were validated using MS lesions datasets.

The rising adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) threatens to impair the stability of power distribution networks. This study examines EV charging behaviors to analyze their impact on grid resilience, focusing on a post-disaster scenario where utility companies charge private EVs at reduced rates. Following an outage, a mass, simultaneous influx of power from affected drivers can create severe congestion and infrastructure stress. To address this, a Nonparametric Short-Term Load Forecasting model is employed, combined with a Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning approach, to design an optimal charging strategy that minimizes congestion while satisfying EV demand. Numerical results based on an adjusted IEEE 30-node test case confirm that coordinated charging significantly improves overall grid efficiency.

The results indicate that Optane DC PM achieves performance levels substantially surpassing those of conventional enterprise-class DRAM. Furthermore, it demonstrates an excellent balance across multiple enterprise metrics, including cost-per-byte, initial acquisition cost, I/O operational expenses, data endurance, rebustness, and overall system efficiency. Optane DC PM supports online expansion, allows for in-place firmware updates without downtime, and ensures instantaneous system boot times following an unplanned power loss, facilitating seamless operations and preventing service interruptions.

Finite element, finite difference, and spectral methods produce the large sparse linear systems commonly associated with time-stepping schemes for parabolic or hyperbolic time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs). The approach leverages one-dimensional (1D) geometric multigrid (MG) techniques, but replaces standard coarse-grid restriction and interpolation stencils with those derived from the discrete orthogonal transformations used in the corresponding coarse-grid transition. This map provides a probabilistic framework to adaptively weigh the two approaches—prioritizing the data-driven model where appropriate while leveraging the regularization properties of the physics-based one where needed. Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) serves as the graph-optimized, localized version of traditional Fisher Discriminant Analysis. Unlike global methods, which seek a single linear transformation for the entire dataset, LFDA maps data into a many-to-one nonlinear framework where linear projections are calculated separately within disjoint partitions or neighborhoods. Because of this neighborly decomposition, LFDA is highly versatile and effective across various analytical contexts, involving both categorical targets with nominal characteristics and continuous targets with structured distributions.

However, despite its adaptability, evaluating the performance of LFDA remains challenging. This difficulty stems from the intrinsic nonlinearity of the resulting transformations and the resulting scatter of points in the target space, particularly within multi-class scenarios. In response, the **lfda** package has been released to provide a user-friendly interface in R (version 4.0+) to implement LFDA. Its primary function, `lfda()`, performs the actual transformation while a supporting `plot()` method generates performance assessments. These visuals are designed to reveal intrinsic data manifolds and projective structures regardless of whether the target variables are nominal or numeric. Consequently, researchers can more effectively evaluate how well LFDA separates classes, maintains cluster cohesion, handles potential overlaps, and preserves or reorganizes numerical associations.
